thread.title: Apple's China Troubles Are In Large Part Temporary - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Paulo Santos
title: Apple's China Troubles Are In Large Part Temporary - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Yesterday, Apple ( AAPL ) announced a significant downward revision to its revenue guidance. Apple blamed most of this downward revision on China:
While we anticipated some challenges in key emerging markets, we did not foresee the magnitude of the economic deceleration, particularly in Greater China. In fact, most of our revenue shortfall to our guidance, and over 100 percent of our year-over-year worldwide revenue decline, occurred in Greater China across iPhone, Mac and iPad.
…
China’s economy began to slow in the second half of 2018. The government-reported GDP growth during the September quarter was the second lowest in the last 25 years. We believe the economic environment in China has been further impacted by rising trade tensions with the United States. As the climate of mounting uncertainty weighed on financial markets, the effects appeared to reach consumers as well, with traffic to our retail stores and our channel partners in China declining as the quarter progressed. And market data has shown that the contraction in Greater China’s smartphone market has been particularly sharp.
The way the Apple letter read, it would seem generic economic weakness, helped by rising trade tensions with the U.S., led to the significant decline in local sales. I believe this is wrong .
It’s not there isn’t an unfavorable economic growth background or that the Chinese smartphone marketplace isn’t weak. Both are true, as can be seen from falling automobile sales, as well as an already weak smartphone market during Q3 2018:
Source: Counterpoint Research
However, there's something else for which there is precedent, which must have hit Apple as well. A factor much stronger than any short-term economic weakness.
The More Relevant Factor I'm talking about the nationalistic reaction of the Chinese consumer to the trade tensions themselves, in what regards the purchase of obvious U.S. brands, with Apple being one of the most obvious. Trade tensions certainly already gave rise to this effect (earlier in the quarter). Then on Dec. 6, the Canadian arrest of Huawei’s CFO certainly reinforced such a trend significantly.
You see, right after that widely-reported event, we got evidence of a well-publicized boycott on Apple’s iPhone sales. Generally speaking, U.S. goods were always at risk of retaliation by the Chinese consumer, but it involving Huawei, one of the largest smartphone competitors to Apple, focused attention on Apple and the iPhone.
Precedent There was precedent to this event. A less obvious diplomatic incident back in 2012 led to a severe drop in Japanese car sales in China:
Toyota said sales of new vehicles in China dropped 48.9% in September from a year earlier to 44,100 vehicles. Honda said that September sales plunged 40.5% to 33,931 vehicles. China sales for Nissan slid 35% last month to 76,100 vehicles.
If that smaller incident led to such deep drops, it’s easy to see Apple might have experienced similar or worse during December, prompting Apple’s significantly revised guidance.
Of course, there will be many more contributing factors, including:
The already-cited lower economic growth and consumer retrenchment. The smartphone market showing some maturity signs, with overall smartphone sales decreasing. A growing competition by very capable $150-$300 Android smartphones in China. The widening of the price gap between those every more capable smartphones and Apple’s flagships. Apple’s flagships now easily cost $1,000, even as capabilities converge. However, from the magnitude of the prior precedent - with car sales for several brands down 35-50% - we can see that the Chinese consumer’s “nationalistic response” likely overwhelmed all other factors.
Now that response made for some very ugly guidance by Apple. But at the same time, there’s a bit of a silver lining : The Chinese consumer forgot about that 2012 diplomatic incident and went back to purchasing Japanese cars. In time, the Chinese consumer also will forget about the U.S. trade war and the Huawei episode. This is made even more likely because in the next few months we should see a trade deal between China and the U.S. resolving the current trade war.
Conclusion The market is generalizing Apple’s horrid guidance to mean China’s weakness is much deeper than it really is.
However, there’s reason and precedent to believe that a large chunk of Apple’s China disaster was prompted by a nationalistic response by the Chinese consumer. If history repeats and the trade war is resolved, it’s very likely that this consumer reaction will quickly fade.
That’s not to say that there aren’t challenges to the iPhone as well as an economic slowdown in China, of course. But given the magnitude of the precedent, I’d say that the main cause for Apple’s massacre is temporary.
